II. 
BACKGROUND 
1 
Q. 
What is the background for this proceeding? 
2 
A. 
[Blazunas, Schafer, and Hammer] On December 18, 2025, the Commission issued its 
3 
order in PJM Interconnection. L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217, at P 193 (2025) (“Order”). In 
4 
the Order, the Commission found that PJM’s Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) 
5 
“is unjust and unreasonable because it does not contain provisions addressing with 
6 
sufficient clarity or consistency the rates, terms, and conditions of service that apply to 
7 
generators serving Co-Located Load and Eligible Customers taking transmission service 
8 
on behalf of Co-Located Load.”1 Specifically, the Commission found PJM’s Tariff “unjust 
9 
and unreasonable because it does not include types of transmission service that reflect 
10 
Eligible Customers taking service on behalf of Co-Located Loads that are willing and able 
11 
to limit their use of the transmission system under certain conditions.”2
12 
The Commission ordered PJM to offer three new forms of transmission service 
13 
under its Tariff, and identified these three new forms of transmission service as: (i) Firm 
14 
Contract Demand transmission service; (ii) Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission 
15 
service; and (iii) interim, non-firm transmission service. The Commission also established 
16 
a paper hearing to determine the just and reasonable rates, terms, and conditions for these 
17 
new transmission services. The paper hearing process provides for initial briefs, responses 
18 
to initial briefs, and replies to those responses. 
19

III.  
PURPOSE OF TESTIMONY 
1 
Q. 
What is the purpose of your testimony?  
2 
A.   
[Blazunas, Schafer, and Hammer] The PJM Transmission Owners, acting through the 
3 
Section 205 Working Group,3 have developed rate design proposals in response to the 
4 
Order’s requirement that PJM implement new transmission services and for submission in 
5 
the paper hearing process.4 The purpose of this testimony is to describe and support the 
6 
PJM Transmission Owners’ rate design proposals for the three new transmission services 
7 
the Commission required in the Order. We also support the PJM Transmission Owners’ 
8 
rate design proposals for a new Grid Reliance Charge. We also address penalty provisions 
9 
and planning and operational issues relating to Eligible Customers5 that choose to take one 
10 
or more of these new services. In particular, we discuss appropriate practices and 
11 
requirements relating to protective systems and other components that will be necessary to 
12 
ensure ongoing system reliability. 
13 
3
The Section 205 Working Group is established under the authority of the Transmission Owner Agreement 
Administrative Committee (“TOAAC”) pursuant to the Consolidated Transmission Owners Agreement (“CTOA”).  
See CTOA § 8.1. These proposals have not yet been submitted to the TOAAC for approval. 
4
For purposes of this testimony and the accompanying responses to the Commission’s paper hearing 
questions, the PJM Transmission Owners are: American Electric Power Service Corporation on behalf of its affiliates, 
Appalachian Power Company, Indiana Michigan Power Company, Kentucky Power Company, Kingsport Power 
Company, Ohio Power Company, Wheeling Power Company, AEP Appalachian Transmission Company, AEP 
Indiana Michigan Transmission Company, AEP Kentucky Transmission Company, AEP Ohio Transmission 
Company, and AEP West Virginia Transmission Company; The Dayton Power and Light Company d/b/a AES Ohio; 
Duquesne Light Company; Dominion Energy Services, Inc. on behalf of Virginia Electric and Power Company d/b/a 
Dominion Energy Virginia; Duke Energy Business Services, LLC for Duke Energy Kentucky, Inc. and Duke Energy 
Ohio, Inc.; East Kentucky Power Cooperative; Exelon Corporation on behalf of its affiliates Atlantic City Electric 
Company, Baltimore Gas and Electric Company, Commonwealth Edison Company, Commonwealth Edison 
Company of Indiana, Inc., Delmarva Power & Light Company, PECO Energy Company (“PECO”), and Potomac 
Electric Power Company; FirstEnergy Service Company, on behalf of its affiliates American Transmission Systems, 
Incorporated, Jersey Central Power & Light Company, Mid-Atlantic Interstate Transmission LLC, The Potomac 
Edison Company, Monongahela Power Company, Keystone Appalachian Transmission Company, and Trans-
Allegheny Interstate Line Company (collectively, the “FirstEnergy Companies”); PPL Electric Utilities Corporation; 
Public Service Electric and Gas Company (“PSE&G”); Rockland Electric Company; and the Southern Maryland 
Electric Cooperative (“SMECO”). 
5
All capitalized terms that are not otherwise defined herein shall have the meaning set forth in the PJM Tariff 
or Amended and Restated Operating Agreement of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.

IV. 
NEW TRANSMISSION SERVICE CATEGORIES AND RATE DESIGNS 
1 
A. 
Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service 
2 
Q. 
What is Firm Contract Demand transmission service?   
3 
A.  
[Blazunas] Pursuant to the Order, under the new Firm Contract Demand transmission 
4 
service (“Firm Contract Demand Service”), Eligible Customers will have the right to 
5 
request transmission service on behalf of a Co-Located Load up to a specified megawatt 
6 
(“MW”) quantity (“Firm Contract Demand”). The Firm Contract Demand Service will 
7 
have the same reservation and curtailment priority as existing firm transmission services at 
8 
the level of the contract demand. However, unlike Network Integration Transmission 
9 
Service (“NITS”) customers, the Eligible Customer taking Firm Contract Demand Service 
10 
on behalf of the Co-Located Load is not permitted to withdraw energy from the PJM 
11 
transmission system beyond the firm contract demand level under this service.  
12 
Q. 
What is the PJM Transmission Owners’ proposed rate design for the new Firm 
13 
Contract Demand Service? 
14 
A. 
[Blazunas] The PJM Transmission Owners propose that the rate for Firm Contract 
15 
Demand Service be based on zonal NITS rates and the underlying NITS revenue 
16 
requirements. Under this approach, Eligible Customers taking Firm Contract Demand 
17 
Service will pay the same base charge per MW as NITS customers, except that, unlike 
18 
NITS customers, their applicable billing determinant will be their specified firm contract 
19 
demand. The transmission charge for a Firm Contract Demand Service customer will be 
20 
calculated by multiplying: (i) the customer’s firm contract demand amount (in MWs) by 
21 
(ii) the applicable zonal NITS rate.   
22

Exhibit No. PTO-0001 
Page 6 of 39 
In zones with formula transmission rates, the single annual rate applicable to both 
1 
NITS and Firm Contract Demand Service customers will be established in the same manner 
2 
as NITS rates are today.6 This rate will be calculated based on each transmission owner’s 
3 
annual net revenue requirement, as determined pursuant to the formula rates contained in 
4 
Attachment H to the PJM Tariff, divided by the single zonal coincident peak load, which 
5 
will include NITS customer load, the total contract demand for all Firm Contract Demand 
6 
Service customers, and load associated with interim, non-firm transmission service.7 This 
7 
will result in a single $/MW-year rate that will apply to both NITS and Firm Contract 
8 
Demand Service customers.   
9 
Eligible Customers will also pay a Grid Reliance Charge for the portion of their 
10 
remaining on-site load not covered by Firm Contract Demand Service. The Grid Reliance 
11 
Charge is discussed in further detail below.   
12 
The procedures for establishing zonal NITS/Firm Contract Demand transmission 
13 
service rates and updating the underlying annual revenue requirements will remain 
14 
unchanged, and Firm Contract Demand Service customers will be treated the same as NITS 
15 
customers under each PJM Transmission Owner’s formula rate protocols.   
16 
A detailed example showing how the Firm Contract Demand Service rate and other 
17 
charges associated with the new services will be calculated is set forth below. 
18 
6
A handful of PJM transmission owners continue to utilize stated rates, which in some cases are based on 
black-box settlements, which may need to be accounted for in specific stated rates for the new firm and non-firm 
contract demand services. 
7
Any changes to a transmission owner’s procedure for assigning a Network Service Peak Load (“NSPL”) tag 
to a Load Serving Entity (“LSE”) may need to be addressed in a future filing.

Exhibit No. PTO-0001 
Page 7 of 39 
Q. 
Why are the PJM Transmission Owners proposing to base the rate for Firm Contract 
1 
Demand Service on the NITS rate, as opposed to the firm Point-to-Point rate or some 
2 
other rate? 
3 
A. 
[Blazunas] The PJM Transmission Owners are proposing to charge the same rate for Firm 
4 
Contract Demand Service and NITS because the level of service provided to both 
5 
customers is, for all relevant purposes, the same. Both NITS and Firm Contract Demand 
6 
Service are firm services for which Network Upgrades will be planned and constructed as 
7 
necessary, with the only difference being that upgrades for NITS customers are identified 
8 
based on anticipated load growth while upgrades for Firm Contract Demand Service 
9 
customers will be identified based on their contracted demand level. Firm Contract 
10 
Demand Service customers will be able to serve their contracted demand through capacity 
11 
procured by PJM just like NITS customers and will not be required to designate specific 
12 
points of receipt and delivery.   
13 
There is no need or benefit to utilizing existing Firm Point-to-Point Service 
14 
(“PTPS”) rates. Firm PTPS rates are generally based on the same revenue requirement as 
15 
the NITS rate, and the nature of Firm Contract Demand Service as contemplated in the 
16 
Order is essentially a variation of NITS service with a specified contract demand level. The 
17 
Firm Contract Demand Service customer will be serving its full contract demand from all 
18 
resources on the grid, not on a point-to-point basis. Consequently, PJM will treat Firm 
19 
Contract Demand Service load during system emergencies in the same manner as load 
20 
using NITS, thus providing service to the Firm Contract Demand Service load on a 
21 
comparable basis with NITS load. Furthermore, Firm Contract Demand transmission 
22 
Service will enjoy the same firmness as NITS load, as well as the same ability to make use 
23

Exhibit No. PTO-0001 
Page 8 of 39 
of PJM resources to serve their full contract demand and ensure guaranteed grid energy 
1 
delivery. Given the similarities between NITS and Firm Contract Demand Service, it would 
2 
be inappropriate to charge Firm Contract Demand Service customers a rate lower than one 
3 
based on the NITS rate because doing so would result in subsidizing these customers at the 
4 
expense of other ratepayers.    
5 
Finally, in PJM, PTPS is generally only utilized for purposes of service at the PJM 
6 
border. That will not be the case for Co-Located Load customers taking Firm Contract 
7 
Demand Service to serve their on-site, contract demand within PJM. Basing the rate for 
8 
Firm Contract Demand Service on the zonal NITS rate also has the advantage of 
9 
minimizing changes to current PJM billing and settlements practices. As it does for NITS 
10 
now, for Firm Contract Demand Service, PJM will perform the billing function for 
11 
transmission, capacity, and energy charges, while electric distribution companies will 
12 
perform their current roles of submitting the metrics that PJM uses to calculate those 
13 
charges, such as customers’ peak load share information.  
14 
Q. 
Do the PJM Transmission Owners have suggestions regarding interconnection 
15 
requirements or operational practices that are necessary for an Eligible Customer to 
16 
take Firm Contract Demand Service on behalf of Co-Located Load? 
17 
A. 
[Hammer] Yes. The PJM Transmission Owners have identified several requirements and 
18 
operational considerations that are necessary to ensure the reliable operation of the Bulk 
19 
Electric System and consistency with established planning and operational practices. In 
20 
particular, the provision of Firm Contract Demand Service on behalf of Co‑Located Load 
21 
should be conditioned on demonstrating that such load is physically and operationally 
22 
capable of being managed in a manner consistent with its firm service designation.  
23

Exhibit No. PTO-0001 
Page 9 of 39 
Accordingly, the PJM Transmission Owners recommend the Commission adopt 
1 
requirements that may include, among other things: (1) compliance with applicable 
2 
interconnection requirements, including the ability to control and measure load consistent 
3 
with PJM operating needs; (2) demonstrated capability to respond to curtailment or 
4 
operational instructions, including the ability to reduce or interrupt loads as necessary to 
5 
support system reliability; and (3) adherence to defined operating practices, including 
6 
telemetry, metering, and communications requirements necessary for real‑time monitoring 
7 
and control.  
8 
In addition, further consideration may also be warranted in a transmission 
9 
constrained area where a significant amount of Co-Located Load taking Firm Contract 
10 
Demand Service relies on operational controls, such as Special Protection Schemes 
11 
(“SPS”) and Remedial Action Schemes (“RAS”), to curtail load back to the level of 
12 
contract demand following the loss of on-site generation. In such circumstances, customers 
13 
may be required to either take a higher level of contract demand or to take NITS for their 
14 
gross load, because the risk of simultaneous SPS/RAS failure in the local area may be 
15 
elevated and could result in cascading grid failure.   
16 
Q. 
What are appropriate mechanisms for an anti-toggling feature for Firm Contract 
17 
Demand Service? 
18 
A. 
[Blazunas] Pursuant to the Order, Firm Contract Demand Service will have a minimum 
19 
term of one year. However, as the Commission recognized, there are concerns regarding a 
20 
customer’s ability to toggle between firm and non-firm service levels.8 There also is a 
21 
concern that Firm Contract Demand Service customers will cause the need for transmission 
22 
8
Order at P 213.

Exhibit No. PTO-0001 
Page 10 of 39 
upgrades and capacity resource procurement to accommodate their Firm Contract Demand 
1 
Service and then exit the system, thereby shifting costs to other customers.9 To partially 
2 
address these concerns, the PJM Transmission Owners recommend a five-year minimum 
3 
commitment period for Firm Contract Demand Service, consistent with the five-year 
4 
minimum commitment noted by the Commission for loads seeking to procure their own 
5 
capacity.10
6 
Q. 
Do the PJM Transmission Owners have a proposal with respect to notice obligations? 
7 
A. 
[Blazunas] Yes. With respect to notice obligations, the PJM Transmission Owners suggest 
8 
that the Commission adopt the same requirements that currently apply to notices of 
9 
termination for NITS under Section 2.5 of the PJM Tariff.11
10 
B. 
Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service 
11 
Q. 
What is Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service?   
12 
A.   
[Blazunas] Under the Order, the Commission established a new Non-Firm Contract 
13 
Demand transmission service (“Non-Firm Contract Demand Service”) to be offered to 
14 
Eligible Customers taking service on behalf of Co-Located Loads. This new service will 
15 
permit Eligible Customers taking service on behalf of such loads to seek to withdraw 
16

2 
Pursuant to the Order, the new Non-Firm Contract Demand Service will be

Service). Under this service, Eligible Customers may reserve transmission service on

behalf of a Co-Located Load as needed during normal, non-emergency system operating

conditions.   
8 
As specified in the Order, reservations for Non-Firm Contract Demand Service will 
9

10 
firm transmission service options in the PJM Tariff. Moreover, reservations will be 
11 
available for terms ranging from one hour to one month, consistent with the terms available 
12 
for non-firm PTPS currently in the PJM Tariff. Finally, Eligible Customers may use Non-
13 
Firm Contract Demand Service to make use of the transmission system above their Firm 
14 
Contract Demand Service level, if transmission capacity is available.13
15 
Q. 
What is the PJM Transmission Owners’ proposed rate design for the new Non-Firm 
16 
Contract Demand Service? 
17 
A. 
[Blazunas] As with Firm Contract Demand Service, the PJM Transmission Owners 
18 
propose that the rate design for Non-Firm Contract Demand Service be based on zonal 
19 
NITS rates in PJM. Under this approach, the maximum rate for Non-Firm Contract 
20 
Demand Service on behalf of Co-Located Load will be calculated by multiplying (i) their 
21

1 
rate. In the same manner as non-firm PTPS today, PJM will have the ability to offer a 
2 
discount off of this maximum rate based on rules and criteria established by the PJM 
3 
Transmission Owners. 
4 
Finally, as with Firm Contract Demand transmission service, Eligible Customers 
5 
taking Non-Firm Contract Demand Service also will pay a Grid Reliance Charge 
6 
representing the remaining on-site load not covered by either Firm Contract Demand 
7 
Service or Non-Firm Contract Demand Service. The base rate for Non-Firm Contract 
8 
Demand Service is adjusted to reflect the impact of the Grid Reliance Charge in order to 
9 
prevent double-recovery. The Grid Reliance Charge is discussed in further detail below. 
10 
A detailed example of the calculation of the Non-Firm Contract Demand Service 
11 
rate and other new service charges is set forth below.  
12 
Q. 
Why is it appropriate to use the same rate for Firm Contract Demand Service to 
13 
establish the maximum rate for the Non-Firm Contract Demand Service? 
14 
A. 
[Blazunas] For the reasons outlined above with respect to Firm Contract Demand Service, 
15 
using the applicable zonal NITS rate to establish the base rate for Non-Firm Contract 
16 
Demand Service is appropriate. In addition, using the same maximum base rate for Firm 
17 
Contract Demand Service and Non-Firm Contract Demand Service is just and reasonable. 
18 
The Commission has traditionally permitted non-firm PTPS to be priced up to (but not 
19 
above) the rate used for firm PTPS,14 and many transmission owners have identical

Q. 
How do the PJM Transmission Owners propose to treat the revenues received from 
5 
Non-Firm Contract Demand Service charges? 
6 
A. 
[Blazunas] To ensure against double recovery, all revenues received from Non-Firm 
7 
Contract Demand Service charges will be credited to NITS and Firm Contract Demand 
8 
Service customers based on their share of the coincident peak load, inclusive of the contract 
9 
demand associated with Firm Contract Demand Service, of the zone where the Co-Located 
10 
Load is physically located. These credits will reduce the total transmission costs for these 
11 
customers, and ensure that these customers, who pay rates based on all of the costs of the 
12 
transmission system, receive the credits associated with Non-Firm Contract Demand 
13 
Service customers’ use of excess capacity on that system. The credits will be applied to 
14 
NITS and Firm Contract Demand Service customers through their PJM bills. This will 
15 
minimize or eliminate the need for the PJM Transmission Owners to modify their formula 
16 
rates.

Interim, Non-Firm Transmission Service 
18 
Q. 
What is interim, non-firm transmission service?  
19 
A.  
[Blazunas] Under the Order, interim, non-firm transmission service, also sometimes 
20 
referred to as “Interim NITS,” allows an Eligible Customer that has requested NITS on 
21 
behalf of a Co-Located Load to take non-firm transmission service that can be interrupted 
22 
until the network upgrades necessary to provide NITS are complete and the Co-Located

1 
Q. 
What are NERC’s transmission planning standards and why is transmission owner 
2 
and transmission provider compliance with those standards important? 
3 
A. 
[Hammer] The North American Electric Reliability Corporation’s (“NERC”) 
4 
Transmission Planning (“TPL”) standards establish mandatory planning requirements to 
5 
ensure the Bulk Electric System can reliably withstand credible contingencies over 
6 
planning horizons. TPL-001 Transmission System Planning Performance Requirements is 
7 
the foundational and currently enforceable transmission planning standard. Its purpose is 
8 
to ensure that the Bulk Electric System is planned so it will operate reliably across a broad 
9 
range of system conditions and contingencies, from normal conditions to extreme events.   
10 
Compliance with the NERC TPL-001 requirements is important because they 
11 
ensure the transmission system is planned to reliably withstand credible outages and system 
12 
stresses, reducing the risk of cascading failures and large-scale blackouts. For transmission 
13 
owners and providers, TPL-001 compliance also minimizes regulatory and financial risk, 
14 
supports coordinated regional planning, and provides a defensible technical basis for 
15 
transmission investments needed to maintain long-term grid reliability. 
16 
Q. 
Does the Order’s proposal to rely on SPS/RAS to accommodate Co-Located Load 
17 
transmission service requests present any reliability or planning concerns? 
18 
A. 
[Hammer] Yes. Under the principle of TPL-001, transmission planners must plan for load 
19 
that has the ability to draw power from the transmission system, not merely for load that is 
20 
expected or intended to do so under normal operating conditions. Reliance on SPS/RAS as 
21 
a substitute for timely network upgrades raises significant concerns under established good 
22 
utility practices and applicable NERC reliability standards. SPS/RAS are generally 
23

Exhibit No. PTO-0001 
Page 34 of 39 
intended as supplemental or last-resort reliability measures, not a primary tool to 
1 
accommodate incremental transmission services on a routine or ongoing basis. In 
2 
particular, substituting SPS/RAS for network upgrade identification, design, coordination, 
3 
testing, and commissioning risks undermining the transparency and predictability of the 
4 
transmission planning process. Transmission Owners must ensure that all applicable 
5 
performance requirements under NERC Standard TPL‑001 remain satisfied, including 
6 
under stressed system conditions and under reasonable worst‑case assumptions such as 
7 
SPS/RAS failure, mis-operation, or unavailability. 
8 
Accordingly, any planning assumptions that rely on SPS/RAS must demonstrate 
9 
acceptable system performance both with and without successful SPS/RAS operation.  
10 
Absent such demonstrations, reliance on SPS/RAS to accommodate Co‑Located Load 
11 
transmission service requests could defer necessary upgrades, increase operational risk, 
12 
and impede prudent transmission planning and reliable operation of the Bulk Electric 
13 
System. 
14 
Q. 
Are there any other grid challenges associated with utilizing SPS/RAS to ensure 
15 
reliability in connection with Co-Located Load taking contract demand transmission 
16 
service? 
17 
A.  
[Hammer] Yes. SPS/RAS are operational tools rather than transmission facilities. While 
18 
they can be effective when properly designed and operated, they introduce dependencies 
19 
related to system protection performance, communications, and coordination during 
20 
stressed system conditions. Individual SPS/RAS-backed Firm Contract Demand Service 
21 
requests may appear manageable in isolation; however, the cumulative impact of multiple 
22 
large Firm Contract Demand Service loads relying on SPS/RAS – particularly within the 
23

Exhibit No. PTO-0001 
Page 35 of 39 
same transmission constrained area – may present risks that are not fully reflected in 
1 
existing planning models. 
2 
There is also a broader planning precedent concern. If major reliability drivers 
3 
identified in planning are routinely mitigated through SPS/RAS in lieu of network 
4 
upgrades, clarification is needed regarding the boundaries of this approach. Specifically, 
5 
stakeholders should understand when infrastructure investment becomes necessary 
6 
regardless of a customer’s willingness to curtail, particularly as load magnitude, geographic 
7 
concentration, and/or system stress increases. 
8 
Q. 
Given these grid challenges, what steps can PJM and the PJM Transmission Owners 
9 
take to ensure grid reliability while relying on SPS/RAS to provide contract demand 
10 
transmission service?  
11 
A. 
[Hammer] To ensure that any reliance on SPS/RAS remains consistent with transmission 
12 
planning practices and applicable reliability standards, the Commission should permit PJM 
13 
and the PJM Transmission Owners to implement necessary guardrails in several areas, 
14 
including: 
15 

Clearly defined eligibility criteria for Firm Contract Demand Service supported by 
16 
SPS/RAS; 
17 

Full redundancy of SPS/RAS, which could include permitting PJM Transmission 
18 
Owners to require the implementation of SPS or RAS on the Transmission Owner’s 
19 
side of the point of interconnection; 
20 

Established reasonable limits on the size, aggregation, and geographic concentration of 
21 
the use of SPS/RAS; 
22

Exhibit No. PTO-0001 
Page 36 of 39 

Defined thresholds under which network upgrades are required notwithstanding the 
1 
availability of operational curtailment; and 
2 

Appropriate rules as to how SPS/RAS supported contract demand service is evaluated 
3 
in PJM’s transmission planning study and PJM Transmission Owners’ interconnection 
4 
facilities studies. 
5 
Implementation of contract demand transmission services must preserve the integrity of 
6 
the transmission planning process and continued compliance with NERC reliability 
7 
standards. From the transmission owners’ perspective, the central implementation issue is 
8 
how reliance on SPS/RAS is appropriately bounded, monitored, and integrated into 
9 
planning and study analyses to ensure that firm transmission service obligations do not 
10 
increasingly depend on operational controls in lieu of durable network infrastructure 
11 
solutions. 
12 
Q. 
Please explain the above-mentioned “full redundancy of SPS/RAS” in more detail. 
13 
A. 
[Hammer] In this context, “full redundancy of SPS/RAS” refers to a layered protection 
14 
framework under which reliability risks associated with Co‑Located Load taking the new 
15 
contract demand transmission services are addressed through both primary, 
16 
customer‑owned protection and an optional, transmission‑owner‑owned backstop, rather 
17 
than reliance on a single protection scheme.  
18 
Under this framework, the primary responsibility for limiting withdrawals from the 
19 
transmission system remains with the interconnection customer or Co‑Located Load, 
20 
typically through customer-owned SPS/RAS that are designed, operated, and maintained 
21 
in accordance with applicable NERC standards and reviewed by PJM. To help accomplish 
22 
this, the Commission should direct NERC to establish requirements that Co-Located Load 
23

Exhibit No. PTO-0001 
Page 37 of 39 
Customers register with NERC so that those customers may be responsible for meeting 
1 
NERC’s reliability standards. These customer‑owned schemes serve as the first line of 
2 
defense and are expected to operate under normal and reasonably foreseeable contingency 
3 
conditions. 
4 
“Full redundancy” does not mean duplicative or parallel protection for every 
5 
contingency, nor does it imply that transmission owners must install SPS/RAS in all cases. 
6 
Rather, it means that, where system studies identify elevated reliability risk, transmission 
7 
owners should have the option to implement a transmission-owner-owned SPS/RAS as a 
8 
secondary backstop to protect the Bulk Electric System in the event of customer‑owned 
9 
scheme failure, mis-operation, or unavailability. 
10 
Q. 
How does this concept of redundancy align with NERC reliability standards, 
11 
including PRC-012? 
12 
A.  
[Hammer] This approach is fully consistent with NERC Reliability Standard PRC‑012, 
13 
which expressly contemplates that SPS/RAS may be owned by Transmission Owners, 
14 
Generator Owners, or Distribution Providers, provided that ownership and accountability 
15 
are clearly defined. Importantly, PRC‑012 does not prohibit multiple SPS/RAS acting on 
16 
the same system condition, nor does it require exclusive reliance on a single owner’s 
17 
protection scheme. Allowing a Transmission Owner to own and operate a backstop 
18 
SPS/RAS therefore fits within the PRC‑012 framework. 
19 
Q. 
Why is reliance on a single, customer‑owned SPS/RAS insufficient in some cases? 
20 
A.  
[Hammer] Transmission planning and operating standards, including TPL‑001, require 
21 
planners to account for credible contingencies and protection system failures, including 
22 
single points of failure and mis-operations. In configurations where Co‑Located Load 
23

Exhibit No. PTO-0001 
Page 38 of 39 
depends on SPS/RAS to limit transmission system withdrawals, exclusive reliance on a 
1 
single, customer‑controlled protection scheme can introduce reliability risk, particularly if 
2 
the equipment is unavailable due to outage or maintenance. In high‑impact scenarios, 
3 
failure of the primary SPS/RAS could result in unexpected load appearing on the 
4 
transmission system, potentially leading to overloads, stability concerns, or emergency 
5 
operating actions. A transmission-owner‑owned backstop SPS/RAS provides an additional 
6 
layer of assurance that these risks can be mitigated before they affect other transmission 
7 
customers or system reliability. 
8 
Q. 
Does “full redundancy” shift responsibility or cost from customers to Transmission 
9 
Owners? 
10 
A.  
[Hammer] No. The concept of full redundancy does not shift responsibility away from 
11 
customers. The presence of a transmission-owner‑owned backstop does not relieve 
12 
customers of compliance obligations, nor does it entitle customers to rely on transmission-
13 
owner‑owned protection in lieu of their own facilities. 
14 
Q. 
Why is the ability to selectively curtail load essential to the contract demand 
15 
transmission service framework adopted by the Commission, and how is that 
16 
capability implemented in practice at the point of interconnection? 
17 
A. 
[Hammer] The Commission directed PJM to create contract demand transmission service 
18 
to reflect loads that are willing and able to limit their withdrawals from the transmission 
19 
system. Load taking contract demand transmission service is granted access to the 
20 
transmission system without corresponding reliability reinforcements to support the full 
21 
gross load, therefore, the reliability condition is curtailment.  
22

Exhibit No. PTO-0001 
Page 39 of 39 
Under certain system conditions, PJM and the PJM Transmission Owners have the 
1 
authority to shed the non‑firm portion of load, either preemptively or immediately 
2 
following a contingency. For example, PJM may arm a SPS/RAS to instantaneously drop 
3 
a large block of load upon the trip of the on-site generator, thereby preventing a thermal or 
4 
stability overload. 
5 
Where a point of interconnection serves both firm and non‑firm contract demand, 
6 
the interconnection must be designed to allow selective curtailment. Operationally, this 
7 
typically requires that firm and non‑firm load be served through separate breakers, feeders, 
8 
or other independently controllable facilities. The Transmission Owner may structure the 
9 
interconnection so that the non‑firm portion can be shed without interrupting firm service. 
10 
Examples could include: 
11 

Separate feeder lines or breakers dedicated to firm versus non‑firm load; 
12 

Partial load‑shedding schemes that trip only designated non‑firm MW; or 
13 

For large facilities such as data centers, multiple transformer banks, with some 
14 
designated as “firm service” and others as “non‑firm service,” allowing independent 
15 
tripping. 
16 
Critically, the ability to distinguish and shed the non‑firm portion of load 
17 
independently is a prerequisite for a contract demand service model. Curtailment cannot 
18 
be all‑or‑nothing; the firm portion of load is expected to remain in service except under 
19 
last‑resort system conditions. As a result, compliance may require the installation of special 
20 
protection or control equipment at the substation or within the customer’s facilities. 
21

Does this complete your testimony at this time? 
22 
A. 
[Blazunas, Schafer, and Hammer] Yes.
